Subject: Private deployment requirements + traffic profile (NexaHealth)

Hi Ben,

Thanks for taking this. We're evaluating a private VPC deployment for NexaHealth's inference workloads and need a sizing + performance readout to move procurement and security reviews forward. Short summary of what we expect: 

- Sustained baseline: ~350 QPS (application-level requests/sec) during business hours (US-PST).
- Peak bursts: up to ~1,200 QPS for short windows (1-10 minutes) and multi-hour peaks (~650 QPS) during scheduled campaigns.
- Payload: avg 550 input tokens / 300 output tokens (roughly 850 tokens total per request).
- Latency target: 95th < 400ms for interactive endpoints; background batched jobs can tolerate higher latency.
- Model family: currently evaluating a 70B encoder-decoder variant (we can share model binary later).
- Data egress constraints: all inference must terminate in our VPC; egress to public internet is restricted (audit requirements).

Attached are sample traffic logs and a short requirements PDF (nexa_requirements_v1.pdf, nexa_traffic_samples.zip).

What we need from Redwood: an initial capacity plan (GPU type & counts), expected headroom for burst absorption, warm pool strategy, network egress estimates, and any recommended quantization/profile to meet the latency target. We'd like a short write-up + a quick architecture call this week if possible.

Best,
Aaron
Head of Infrastructure, NexaHealth

Subject: RE: Private deployment requirements + traffic profile (NexaHealth) -- internal sizing draft

Team — pulling initial numbers together for NexaHealth. Summarizing assumptions (from Aaron's note + our follow-up):

- Workload: 70B encoder-decoder; avg 850 tokens/request; target 95th < 400ms for interactive endpoints.
- Baseline sustained: 350 QPS; peak instantaneous: 1,200 QPS; multi-hour peak: 650 QPS.
- We should treat interactive and batch endpoints separately: keep interactive on a low-latency pool, batch on cheaper quantized nodes.

Quick projection (ballpark, conservative):
- Option A (higher perf): A100-80GB (fp16 / qcompress)
  - Per-GPU steady QPS (850 tokens, fp16): ~110 QPS
  - Peak (short-burst handling) safe headroom: provision 12 GPUs => 12 * 110 = 1,320 QPS (good fit for 1,200 peak, leaves ~10% buffer).
  - Warm pool: maintain 2 GPUs kept warm to reduce cold-start impact; autoscale step increments of 2 GPUs.

- Option B (cost optimized): 8x 80GB Ampere-style but quantized (int8) or 16x 48GB T4-style nodes
  - Per-GPU int8 throughput estimate: ~70 QPS
  - To reach 1,200 peak you'd need ~18 GPUs (18 * 70 = 1,260 QPS).
  - Latency at int8 may risk the 95th target depending on kernel stack and sequence-length variance.

Network / egress considerations:
- Estimate per-request egress: ~0.5 KB (payload) + model artifacts negligible during run. Total sustained egress at 1,200 QPS ~ 600 KB/s (~4.8 Mbps) — but for larger batched traffic this scales.
- More significant is inter-node traffic for multiplexing and KV cache; recommend at least 25 Gbps NICs on inference hosts if colocated with multiple GPUs to avoid tail latency when local traffic spikes.

Operational notes:
- Autoscale policy: aggressive scale-up (fast) on CPU queue depth + request latency signal; conservative scale-down with 10–15 minute cooldown to avoid oscillation during campaign bursts.
- Warm pool: aim for 15–20% of peak capacity pre-warmed (for 1,200 peak -> 2–3 GPUs kept ready depending on GPU sizing).
- Fallback: provide a compatible smaller-model variant routed during saturation to guarantee availability with higher latency / reduced quality.

Attached is the capacity_model_v2.xlsx with the numbers/formulas. Next steps: validate the token counts with Aaron, pick a preferred GPU family, and schedule the architecture session for the 9th.

—Ben
